events.passage: COJS entry, paragraphs describing findspot, reused block, dedication and titulature; inscription translation names Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judea.

supportedClaim.en: The Caesarea inscription attests Pilate's title and a building dedication; it does not attest the trial of Jesus.
supportedClaim.es: La inscripción de Cesarea acredita el título de Pilato y una dedicación edilicia; no documenta el proceso de Jesús.

events.limitations: Fragmentary stone reused in a stairway; COJS is a secondary catalog entry. The campaign's 27–36 range is an editorial slice of the conventional prefecture dates, not the inscription's date.

events.passage: Tacitus, Annals 15.44, passage on Christus and the Neronian punishments; DCC notes distinguish Tacitus' report from other evidence and observe Christian sources do not mention an arson charge.

supportedClaim.en: Tacitus, writing decades later, says Christus was executed under Tiberius by Pontius Pilate. The passage does not place the execution in a specific year or record a refuge episode.
supportedClaim.es: Tácito, décadas después, dice que Christus fue ejecutado bajo Tiberio por Poncio Pilato. El pasaje no fija un año concreto ni registra un episodio de refugio.

events.limitations: Retrospective Roman literary testimony, not eyewitness evidence. The 30–33 date is a modern estimate; the episode candidate's 'Christian sources' wording should cite those separately if retained.

events.passage: Galatians 1:18–19: Paul says that after three years he went to Jerusalem, stayed fifteen days with Cephas, and saw James, the Lord's brother.

supportedClaim.en: Paul's letter retrospectively reports a Jerusalem visit and meetings with Cephas and James. It does not establish that a particular group remained in the city immediately after Jesus' death.
supportedClaim.es: La carta de Pablo informa retrospectivamente de una visita a Jerusalén y encuentros con Cefas y Santiago. No demuestra que un grupo concreto permaneciera allí inmediatamente después de la muerte de Jesús.

events.limitations: Paul's own self-presentation in a polemical letter; 'after three years' is relative and does not fix a calendar date or community size.

events.passage: Galatians 1:13–17: Paul recalls persecution, a divine revelation/commission, Arabia, and return to Damascus.

supportedClaim.en: Paul says he persecuted the assembly of God and describes his change as a revelation and commission; he names Arabia and Damascus but gives no complete itinerary or exact year.
supportedClaim.es: Pablo dice que persiguió a la asamblea de Dios y describe su cambio como revelación y encargo; nombra Arabia y Damasco, pero no ofrece itinerario completo ni año exacto.

events.limitations: The revelation is Paul's theological account, not an independently verifiable supernatural event. Year range c.33–36 is reconstructed; do not stage an unreported journey.

events.passage: Galatians 1:18–19, especially Paul's 'fifteen days' and named contacts; Yale Bible Study chronology page consulted for the broader chronology anchor (Gallio/Delphi).

supportedClaim.en: Paul reports a Jerusalem visit, a fifteen-day stay with Cephas, and seeing James.
supportedClaim.es: Pablo informa de una visita a Jerusalén, una estancia de quince días con Cefas y un encuentro con Santiago.

events.limitations: This repeats the preceding episode's source/event and should be made a distinct editorial angle or treated as duplicate. Relative interval and date of Paul's call remain uncertain; the Yale overview does not make the exact year certain.

events.passage: Galatians 2:11–14: Cephas at Antioch; certain people 'from James' arrive; Cephas withdraws from eating with Gentiles; Paul says he confronted him.

supportedClaim.en: Paul's account describes a dispute over table fellowship at Antioch and says Cephas withdrew after people from James arrived.
supportedClaim.es: El relato de Pablo describe una disputa sobre la comida compartida en Antioquía y dice que Cefas se apartó tras la llegada de personas procedentes de Santiago.

events.limitations: Only Paul's account survives here; it does not call them formal envoys or establish the incident's date or outcome. Yale Divinity PDF cited in dossier returned 404; local courier/network reconstruction is fictional, not attested by Galatians.

events.passage: Suetonius, Claudius 25.4: Claudius expels Jews from Rome after disturbances 'impulsore Chresto'. Cambridge scholarly article search result notes scholarly disagreement in dating this incident (41 vs c.49).

supportedClaim.en: Suetonius reports disturbances among Jews in Rome and an expulsion under Claudius, mentioning 'Chrestus'.
supportedClaim.es: Suetonio informa de disturbios entre judíos de Roma y una expulsión bajo Claudio, y menciona a «Chrestus».

events.limitations: The text does not identify Chrestus with Jesus/Christ, specify a year, or show that Christians were the only people expelled. The c.49 date is conventional and debated; this candidate's Christian-conflict reading is a hypothesis.

events.passage: Acts 15:1–29: narrative of a Jerusalem meeting debating circumcision of gentile adherents and a set of requirements; compare Paul's distinct account in Galatians 2:1–10.

supportedClaim.en: Acts narrates a Jerusalem debate about gentile inclusion and circumcision; Paul independently describes a Jerusalem visit and agreement about mission in Galatians 2.
supportedClaim.es: Hechos narra un debate en Jerusalén sobre la inclusión gentil y la circuncisión; Pablo describe por separado una visita y un acuerdo sobre la misión en Gálatas 2.

events.limitations: Acts and Galatians cannot be harmonized into one securely identified meeting without argument; date c.49–50 is reconstructed. The Oxford Handbook page is an overview, not primary evidence; source selection should cite both accounts and signal disagreement.

events.passage: Acts 18:1–18: Paul meets Prisca and Aquila in Corinth, stays eighteen months, and is brought before Gallio; compare Gallio inscription for the proconsul's tenure.

supportedClaim.en: Acts reports Paul working with Prisca and Aquila in Corinth and staying there eighteen months; the Gallio episode provides a chronological anchor.
supportedClaim.es: Hechos informa que Pablo trabajó con Prisca y Aquila en Corinto y permaneció allí dieciocho meses; el episodio de Galión sirve de ancla cronológica.

events.limitations: Narrative source, not a contemporary record of founding. Exact 50–52 dating depends on the Delphi inscription's date and chronology reconstruction; DCC URL listed in selection was unavailable in the earlier consultation.

events.passage: Jewish Annotated New Testament introduction to 1 Thessalonians: dates ca. 50 CE and calls it earliest extant Pauline writing; contrast primary letter itself.

supportedClaim.en: 1 Thessalonians is commonly dated around 50 CE and is the earliest surviving Pauline letter.
supportedClaim.es: 1 Tesalonicenses suele fecharse hacia el año 50 y es la carta paulina conservada más antigua.

events.limitations: The source is scholarly commentary; this supports conventional date/order, not that the letter was written in Corinth. The dossier's OUP source was only an abstract and should not be represented as full-book consultation.

events.passage: Galatians 1–2 and 3:1–5: Paul's argument about his commission, Abraham, law, and gentile belonging; SBL Bible Odyssey link listed in dossier was unavailable in prior consultation.

supportedClaim.en: Galatians preserves a dispute over gentile belonging, circumcision, and the law as argued by Paul.
supportedClaim.es: Gálatas conserva una disputa sobre la pertenencia gentil, la circuncisión y la ley tal como la argumenta Pablo.

events.limitations: The letter itself supports the dispute; neither its place of composition nor c.54–55 is established by these chapters. Ephesus is not securely documented as the writing location.

events.passage: 1 Corinthians 1–16: Paul addresses factions, food, lawsuits, worship, gifts, collection and resurrection in a community he addresses as Corinth.

supportedClaim.en: 1 Corinthians addresses multiple community disputes and practices at Corinth.
supportedClaim.es: 1 Corintios aborda diversas disputas y prácticas comunitarias en Corinto.

events.limitations: Primary letter supports the topics but not the selection's c.54–55 date or Ephesus writing location by itself. OUP abstract is not full-text evidence and should be described only as abstract consulted.

events.passage: Romans 16: Paul commends Phoebe of Cenchreae, greets multiple named people, and mentions a house-church; Romans 1:13 says Paul had often intended to visit Rome.

supportedClaim.en: Romans 16 attests a network of people and communities in Rome and Phoebe's connection to Cenchreae; Paul says he had not yet visited Rome.
supportedClaim.es: Romanos 16 acredita una red de personas y comunidades en Roma y el vínculo de Febe con Cencreas; Pablo dice que aún no había visitado Roma.

events.limitations: It does not itself give composition date/place. Corinth is a scholarly inference; the dossier's Oxford source was an abstract only. The claim 'community he did not found' is supported by Romans 1:13, not chapter 16 alone.

events.passage: Acts 25:10–12: Paul invokes his appeal to Caesar before Festus; Acts 21–26 gives the preceding detention narrative.

supportedClaim.en: In Acts' narrative, Paul appeals to Caesar before Festus while held at Caesarea.
supportedClaim.es: En el relato de Hechos, Pablo apela al César ante Festo mientras está detenido en Cesarea.

events.limitations: This is a theological narrative, not a surviving court transcript. The appeal passage supports the appeal, not every claim about causes, dates, or legal procedure; use Caesarea as scene, not Jerusalem after departure.

events.passage: Tacitus, Annals 15.44, relating the Rome fire, Nero's response, and punishments of Christians; DCC notes source limits and comparison with Suetonius/Pliny.

supportedClaim.en: Tacitus reports that after the Rome fire Nero punished people called Christians and describes Christus' execution under Pilate.
supportedClaim.es: Tácito informa de que, tras el incendio de Roma, Nerón castigó a personas llamadas cristianas y describe la ejecución de Christus bajo Pilato.

events.limitations: Tacitus wrote decades later and is not an eyewitness to the punishment. His account does not prove Christians caused the fire; indeed he portrays the arson charge as a scapegoating measure. No separately documented evacuation/recovery episode.

events.passage: Mark 1:1–15 as opening and narrative evidence for the Gospel's representation of Jesus; Oxford title page is metadata/abstract only, not full-text chapter evidence.

supportedClaim.en: The Gospel of Mark presents a narrative about Jesus and locates its opening in a Second Temple Jewish setting.
supportedClaim.es: El Evangelio de Marcos presenta un relato sobre Jesús y sitúa su comienzo en el contexto judío del Segundo Templo.

events.limitations: Mark's date is commonly placed around the Jewish War but debated; text does not identify its author or place of composition. Do not state that this source proves it was written during the war or in Antioch.

events.passage: Livius summary explicitly cites Josephus, Jewish War 6; primary source locator: Josephus, War 6.4.5–7.1.1 (Temple fire/destruction and capture).

supportedClaim.en: Josephus narrates the Roman capture and destruction of the Jerusalem Temple in 70 CE.
supportedClaim.es: Josefo narra la toma romana y destrucción del Templo de Jerusalén en el año 70.

events.limitations: Josephus is a near-contemporary participant writing under Roman patronage; casualty totals and speeches are rhetorically shaped. Livius is a secondary summary, not the primary source itself.

events.passage: Matthew 1 and Luke 1 as distinct narrative openings; Oxford resource supplied only as abstract/metadata, not evidence for audience reconstruction.

supportedClaim.en: Matthew and Luke preserve distinct narrative presentations of Jesus; their texts can be compared for differing genealogies and infancy narratives.
supportedClaim.es: Mateo y Lucas conservan presentaciones narrativas distintas de Jesús; sus textos permiten comparar genealogías y relatos de infancia diferentes.

events.limitations: The claim that they were tailored for distinct communities is scholarly inference; neither texts nor Oxford abstract consulted here proves specific communities or provenance in Antioch.

events.passage: Didache, especially chapters 7 (baptism), 9–10 (prayers), 11–13 (itinerant teachers/prophets), and 14–15 (assembly and local officers); academic discussion of composite date and provenance consulted via Cambridge HTR abstract.

supportedClaim.en: The Didache contains instructions on baptism, communal prayer, itinerant teachers, and local leadership.
supportedClaim.es: La Didaché contiene instrucciones sobre bautismo, oración comunitaria, maestros itinerantes y liderazgo local.

events.limitations: Its date and place of composition remain disputed; Syrian provenance is a proposal, not established fact. The earlychristianwritings page is an edition/translation resource, while the Cambridge source is abstract only.

events.passage: 1 Clement 1–3 and 47–59: letter addresses the Corinthian church, laments dissension and removal of presbyters, and urges restoration.

supportedClaim.en: 1 Clement is a Roman church's letter urging reconciliation in a leadership conflict at Corinth.
supportedClaim.es: 1 Clemente es una carta de la iglesia de Roma que pide reconciliación en un conflicto de liderazgo en Corinto.

events.limitations: The letter itself does not name its author as Clement; the Roman origin and late-first-century date are conventional early-Christian scholarly reconstructions. The claimed intervention is supported, but exact c.95 date is not stated in the text.

events.passage: Pliny, Letters 10.96–97: Pliny asks Trajan how to handle accused Christians; reports morning meeting, ethical pledge, and meal; Trajan replies not to seek them out.

supportedClaim.en: Pliny asks Trajan about proceedings against accused Christians and reports their pre-dawn meeting and practices.
supportedClaim.es: Plinio consulta a Trajano sobre los procesos contra acusados de cristianismo e informa de sus reuniones antes del alba y prácticas.

events.limitations: Governor's correspondence, not a neutral ethnography; evidence is for Bithynia-Pontus, not a general empire-wide policy. c.112 is inferred from correspondence chronology.

events.passage: Justin, First Apology 65–67, especially 67: Sunday assembly, apostolic memoirs/prophets read, instruction, prayer, bread/wine, collection for those in need.

supportedClaim.en: Justin describes Sunday gatherings, readings, prayer, Eucharist, and collections for people in need.
supportedClaim.es: Justino describe reuniones dominicales, lecturas, oración, eucaristía y colectas para personas necesitadas.

events.limitations: The passage describes Christian practice in general terms; it does not itself establish Justin's teaching location or prove these exact practices were unique to Rome. Apologetic self-description, not a neutral census.

events.passage: Melito, Apology fragments preserved at Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 4.26.5–11; source record gives fragment provenance and bibliographic editions.

supportedClaim.en: Eusebius preserves fragments of a work attributed to Melito and addressed to an emperor, arguing that Christian teaching had benefited the empire.
supportedClaim.es: Eusebio conserva fragmentos de una obra atribuida a Melitón y dirigida a un emperador, donde sostiene que la enseñanza cristiana benefició al imperio.

events.limitations: The fragment does not simply 'denounce measures' in the form asserted by the candidate; it asks the emperor to examine recent anti-Christian measures and appeals to imperial justice. The surviving text is fragmentary, mediated by Eusebius, and date/address details are debated.

events.passage: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 5.1: preserved letter from Christians of Vienne and Lugdunum to Asian and Phrygian communities; narratives of arrest, trial, and deaths.

supportedClaim.en: Eusebius preserves a letter reporting trials and violence against Christians at Lyon and Vienne.
supportedClaim.es: Eusebio conserva una carta que informa de procesos y violencia contra cristianos en Lyon y Vienne.

events.limitations: Eusebius is later than the events and transmits a community letter; date 177 is inferred. The letter has theological rhetoric, visions and miracles that must remain source-attributed, not asserted as verified events.

events.passage: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3.2–3: Roman episcopal succession argument; Book I preface and Book III identify polemical target and tradition claims.

supportedClaim.en: Irenaeus' polemic argues from inherited teaching and episcopal succession, using Rome as an example.
supportedClaim.es: La polémica de Ireneo argumenta desde la enseñanza heredada y la sucesión episcopal, y usa Roma como ejemplo.

events.limitations: This is a theological polemic, not a neutral account of all communities or uncontested institutional history. It supports debate over authority/tradition, not a specific Lyon archival event; composition c.180–200 is external dating.

events.passage: Tertullian, Apologeticum prologue §§1–3 on uninvestigated condemnation; ch.39 on Christian assembly/charity and chs.40–42 on social practice.

supportedClaim.en: Tertullian protests condemnation without inquiry and describes communal worship and care practices.
supportedClaim.es: Tertuliano protesta contra condenas sin investigación y describe culto comunitario y prácticas de asistencia.

events.limitations: The Apology is forensic rhetoric and advocacy, not a neutral legal register. The selection's c.197 date is conventional; ch.39 does not prove specific locations or every practice across Christians.

events.passage: Passion of Perpetua and Felicity §§3–10 (first-person prison visions) and §§16–21 (trial/execution); page introduction dates event 203.

supportedClaim.en: The Passion preserves a near-contemporary Christian account of Perpetua and Felicity's imprisonment and execution at Carthage.
supportedClaim.es: La Pasión conserva un relato cristiano cercano a los hechos sobre el encarcelamiento y ejecución de Perpetua y Felicidad en Cartago.

events.limitations: The work has a complex literary/redactional history and theological vision material; date 203 is conventional and the page's introductory header is secondary. Treat visions as the text's claims, not verified supernatural events.

events.passage: British Library Archives catalogue, Papyrus 2457 / P.Oxy. XII 1464 description: a libellus records Aurelius Gaion, wife, and children performing sacrifice and libation before officials at Oxyrhynchus under Decius.

supportedClaim.en: A surviving Egyptian certificate records a household's sacrifice during Decius' reign, demonstrating documentary compliance with a sacrifice requirement.
supportedClaim.es: Un certificado egipcio conservado registra el sacrificio de una familia durante el reinado de Decio y documenta el cumplimiento de un requisito sacrificial.

events.limitations: The papyrus records this named household only; it does not prove a uniform empire-wide edict or universal enforcement, nor persecution of Christians specifically. Official catalog describes artifact; earlier P.Oxy project URL is broad and did not establish P.Oxy.1464.

events.passage: Cyprian, Epistle 81 §§1–2 (New Advent numbering; also catalogued as Epistle 80): report of Valerian's rescript and executions at Rome; for Cyprian's own arrest/sentence/death consult Pontius, Life and Passion §§15–18, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0505.htm.

supportedClaim.en: Cyprian reports Valerian's anti-clerical order and Roman executions; Pontius narrates Cyprian's arrest, sentence, and execution at Carthage.
supportedClaim.es: Cipriano informa de la orden de Valeriano contra el clero y de ejecuciones en Roma; Poncio narra el arresto, sentencia y ejecución de Cipriano en Cartago.

events.limitations: The letter does not itself attest Cyprian's own death; Pontius' near-contemporary Life/Passion is hagiographic and presents providential framing. Exact 257–258 sequence reconstructed from multiple sources; distinguish exile/first edict from execution under second edict.

events.passage: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 8.2–3 and 8.5: orders against churches/scriptures and subsequent punishments, with Eusebius' explicitly Christian narrative frame.

supportedClaim.en: Eusebius records the Great Persecution's measures against churches and Christian texts and reports punishments in several provinces.
supportedClaim.es: Eusebio registra medidas de la Gran Persecución contra iglesias y textos cristianos, e informa de castigos en varias provincias.

events.limitations: Eusebius is a Christian historian and his rhetoric interprets events providentially; implementation differed by region and date. This source does not document a specific Milan archive or single uniform local event, nor all the 303–313 range.
